VBO:0200971.summary: Adaptability and useful work lie at the heart of the Old Farm Collie tradition. Scottish farm dogs helped herd, guard and drive sheep; modern preservation groups seek to keep that versatility alongside companionship. Their revival followed a twentieth-century decline in these farm collies. As a landrace, the type allows variation while favoring sound, moderate dogs and working ability over show-ring exaggeration.
VBO:0200971.shortDescription: A versatile farm-collie tradition, revived to preserve useful work and companionship within a varied landrace.
VBO:0200971.historicalRoots: Scottish farm-collie landrace; modern preservation revival after twentieth-century decline.

sources.title: UC Davis VGL: Scottish Collie genetic diversity report
sources.evidence: pp2–5: Scottish/Scotch/Old Farm Collie aliases explicitly distinguished from conformation Rough/Smooth Collies. Historic work herding, protecting and driving sheep. Revival after twentieth-century decline aims original form, health/function including sheepherding and hunting; landrace variety and broad functional standard, moderation in head/coat rather than exaggeration. Hardy/versatile work and faithful companionship are intended type qualities, not an experimental temperament finding. SCPS and OTSC restoration populations overlap; OTFS cause incorporated into OTSC, so0973 is not automatically another distinct population.

VBO:0200978.summary: Ori-Pei was developed by Aaron Silver in North America during the 1970s as a smaller companion with Shar-Pei and Pug ancestry. The project continued across several generations, so the name covers descendants of that original pairing rather than one fixed first-generation mix.
VBO:0200978.shortDescription: Developed in North America in the 1970s, this Shar-Pei–Pug companion cross continued through several generations.
VBO:0200978.historicalRoots: North American Shar-Pei/Pug breeding project begun by Aaron Silver in the1970s.

sources.title: Designer Breed Registry Ori-Pei primary text retained from search index
sources.evidence: Retained full primary-page text returned by search index, reported crawl age7.3years; stable history only, not current HTML or present recognition.

sources.title: designer-dogs-cspca.pdf
sources.evidence: Exact Pug/Shar-Pei identity separately from Ori-Pei/Pug Pug-A-Pei.

sources.title: ori-pei-nkc.html
sources.evidence: Current named Ori Pei page only; no character/history claims from page body.

VBO:0200587.summary: Giant Spitz are lively, attentive dogs with close attachment to their people and a watchful response to unfamiliar visitors. They carry on Germany's home-and-farm watchdog tradition, pairing alertness with a receptive approach to learning. The Giant variety stands about 45 cm at the shoulder; brown and black are two of its coat colours.
VBO:0200587.shortDescription: An attentive German watchdog, closely attached to its people, in the larger brown and black Spitz variety.
VBO:0200587.historicalRoots: German home-and-farm watch and companion tradition.

sources.title: FCI Standard97 — German Giant, Medium and Miniature Spitz
sources.evidence: FCI97 20.09.2024, joint Giant/Medium/Miniature section pp8–14: attentive, lively, attached, teachable, watchful around strangers; home/farm watch and companion use. Heights45±5/35±5/27±3cm and exact permitted colours. Temperament is shared across these sizes/colours, not a claim of colour-linked personality.

VBO:0200591.summary: Medium Spitz combine eager learning with a lively, attentive manner and a strong bond to familiar people. Their caution around strangers belongs to a long German tradition of keeping watch over homes and farms. Known as Mittelspitz, they occupy the middle size in the German Spitz family, about 35 cm at the shoulder; brown and black coats occur in this middle size.
VBO:0200591.shortDescription: The Mittelspitz brings alert watchfulness and eager learning to a middle-sized member of Germany's Spitz family.
VBO:0200591.historicalRoots: German watch and companion dogs, in the middle-sized Mittelspitz variety.

sources.title: FCI Standard97 — German Giant, Medium and Miniature Spitz
sources.evidence: FCI97 20.09.2024, joint Giant/Medium/Miniature section pp8–14: attentive, lively, attached, teachable, watchful around strangers; home/farm watch and companion use. Heights45±5/35±5/27±3cm and exact permitted colours. Temperament is shared across these sizes/colours, not a claim of colour-linked personality.

VBO:0200596.summary: Miniature Spitz are animated, watchful companions, attentive to their surroundings and closely attached to their people. Their readiness to learn sits alongside a cautious response to unfamiliar visitors, continuing the German Spitz's home-and-farm watchdog heritage. The Kleinspitz stands about 27 cm at the shoulder, larger than the separately named Toy Spitz or Pomeranian.
VBO:0200596.shortDescription: A small, lively German watchdog whose attachment and alertness accompany a receptive approach to learning.
VBO:0200596.historicalRoots: German watch and companion tradition, in the Kleinspitz size variety.

sources.title: FCI Standard97 — German Giant, Medium and Miniature Spitz
sources.evidence: FCI97 20.09.2024, joint Giant/Medium/Miniature section pp8–14: attentive, lively, attached, teachable, watchful around strangers; home/farm watch and companion use. Heights45±5/35±5/27±3cm and exact permitted colours. Temperament is shared across these sizes/colours, not a claim of colour-linked personality.

VBO:0200607.summary: Giant Schnauzers combine an even, good-natured manner with self-assurance and strong loyalty. They bring trainability, endurance and speed to demanding work. Originally cattle drivers in southern Germany, they entered a stud book in 1913 and were officially recognized as working dogs in 1925. This variety carries a pure black coat and undercoat.
VBO:0200607.shortDescription: An assured, trainable German worker whose cattle-driving background helped shape its strength and endurance.
VBO:0200607.historicalRoots: Southern German cattle-driving dogs, registered from 1913 and recognized for working use in 1925.

sources.title: FCI Standard181 — Giant Schnauzer
sources.evidence: FCI181 10.06.2021: even good-natured temperament, loyalty, intelligence/trainability/endurance/speed; southern German cattle driving, studbook1913, working recognition1925; pure black with black undercoat and natural sabre/sickle tail.

VBO:0200642.summary: Griffon Bruxellois dogs tend to stay closely attached to their people while keeping an alert, proud watch on their surroundings. Their ancestors guarded Brussels carriages and hunted rodents in stables. Topsy and Foxine were the first registered examples in Belgium’s Saint Hubert studbook in 1883; royal interest later helped the breed spread abroad.
VBO:0200642.shortDescription: An alert, proud Brussels companion, often strongly attached to its people, with a carriage-guarding past.
VBO:0200642.historicalRoots: Brussels Smousje descendants with carriage-guarding and stable rodent work; first Saint Hubert studbook entries1883.

sources.title: FCI standards 80/81/82: Griffon Bruxellois, Griffon Belge and Petit Brabançon, 5 May 2003
sources.evidence: Temperament describes alert, proud, very watchful dogs strongly attached to owners. History describes Brussels Smousje, guarding carriages and stable rodent control; Topsy and Foxine were the first Griffon Bruxellois registered in the Saint Hubert studbook in1883, and Belgian royal interest around1900 helped international spread. FCI80 specifically defines red/reddish rough coat, distinguishing rough black/tan FCI81 and smooth FCI82. No coat-specific temperament asserted.

VBO:0200895.summary: Often lively and self-assured, red Miniature Pinschers combine a spirited manner with an even temperament. They were already common in Germany around the turn of the twentieth century, with about 1,300 dogs entered in the 1925 studbook. Solid red and black-and-tan survived the selection from a broader range of earlier colours.
VBO:0200895.shortDescription: An often lively, self-assured German companion whose red variety shares the Miniature Pinscher’s spirited character.
VBO:0200895.historicalRoots: German Miniature Pinscher companion population, numerous by the turn of the twentieth century; selected solid red variety.

sources.title: FCI185 Miniature Pinscher (Zwergpinscher),18 April2007
sources.evidence: Temperament describes lively, spirited, self-assured and evenly tempered. History records many dogs around the turn of the century and1300 studbook entries in1925; solid red/red-brown and black with lighter markings were selected from numerous earlier colours. Utilization is house and companion dog. Self-coloured identity expressly includes deer red, reddish-brown to dark red-brown. Morphology specifies natural tail with sabre or sickle carriage; ears may be prick or high-set forward-folded V-shaped drop ears. Exact FCI185, not190.

VBO:0200941.summary: Usually gentle and composed, yet capable of playfulness, the Landseer Newfoundland belongs to a long tradition of work around boats and water. Newfoundlands hauled loads and served aboard ships; their swimming strength made them valuable for water rescues. The Landseer name remembers Sir Edwin Landseer’s paintings, which helped popularize white-and-black Newfoundlands in the nineteenth century.
VBO:0200941.shortDescription: A usually gentle, composed Newfoundland variety whose Landseer name recalls nineteenth-century paintings.
VBO:0200941.historicalRoots: White-and-black Newfoundland variety named for Sir Edwin Landseer; Canadian draft and ship-dog tradition.

sources.title: Canadian Kennel Club: Newfoundland standard, effective January 2018; 2024 Group 3 edition
sources.evidence: Temperament section defines gentleness, serenity and capacity for fun; Origin & Purpose names lifeguard and draught work. Colour section explicitly defines Landseer Newfoundland as white with black markings, shown in the same classes as black Newfoundlands. Morphology requires massive deep body with mature substance, no legginess, and hanging rudder tail reaching to or below hocks.

sources.title: Newfoundland Dog Club of Canada: About the Newfoundland
sources.evidence: Club history describes native Newfoundland dogs’ gentle dispositions, swimming ability, draft and ship work; white-and-black Newfoundlands became popular after Sir Edwin Landseer’s painting in the mid nineteenth century and took his name. Origin theories are explicitly speculative.

VBO:0201007.summary: Affectionate with familiar people but sometimes reserved with strangers, the miniature Peruvian Hairless Dog is described as lively and alert. Its watchfulness sits alongside a long history as a companion. Known in Peru as the viringo, hairless dogs appear on pre-Inca pottery, including pieces from the Mochica and Chancay cultures. This is the smallest of the breed’s three size varieties.
VBO:0201007.shortDescription: An alert, affectionate companion with familiar people, the smallest viringo carries a history seen in pre-Inca pottery.
VBO:0201007.historicalRoots: Peru is the primary standard’s origin. A dry coastal path is art direction, not a claimed historical subregion or a pottery reconstruction.

sources.title: FCI: Peruvian Hairless Dog standard 310 (26 October 2021)
sources.evidence: Behaviour: affectionate with familiar people, lively and alert, sometimes wary of strangers; watchdog tendency. History: viringo depicted in pre-Inca ceramics including Mochica and Chancay. Size Small 25–40cm and 4–8kg maps catalogue Miniature; not inferred from pixels. No size-specific temperament. Coated and hairless relatives occur in same litters, but no health/therapeutic claim.

VBO:0201058.summary: Loyal, friendly and active, the Standard Poodle combines an eager capacity for learning with close attachment to its people. Its ancestors retrieved wildfowl, and the breed gradually separated from the Barbet as breeders developed a distinctive companion. Grey and fawn Standards share that history and character with the other colours.
VBO:0201058.shortDescription: A loyal, active companion whose quick learning and wildfowl-retrieving past belong to the wider Poodle tradition.

sources.title: FCI Standard172 — Poodle
sources.evidence: FCI172 pp2–3: originally wildfowling, Barbet ancestry and gradual separation; friendly/joyful/loyal, alert/active and capable of learning. pp5–8: high tail set at loin, ideally ten-past-nine carriage relative to topline, docking no longer authorized; grey/fawn includes orange-fawn apricot; Standard over45–60cm(+2), Miniature over28–35cm. These behavioural tendencies are shared across sizes and colours.

VBO:0201244.summary: Slovakian Wire-Haired Pointers are typically receptive to training, with a working style built around searching and retrieving. They work across open ground, woodland and water, with particular emphasis on finding wounded game after a shot. In the field their balanced, lively movement opens into a gallop on the plain.
VBO:0201244.shortDescription: An adaptable Slovak gundog, receptive to training and bred to search fields, woods and water for wounded game.
VBO:0201244.historicalRoots: Slovak pointing and retrieving work across open ground, woodland and water.

sources.title: FCI Standard 320 — Wirehaired Slovakian Pointer
sources.evidence: FCI320 p2 gives obedient/easy-to-train work, plain/woods/water and particular searching/retrieving wounded game after shooting. P4 describes balanced lively gait and galloping on the plain. P3 mature amber eyes, drop ears, long head and historical half-length docking; p5 harsh flat protective coat and brown-shaded sable called grey. No intimate household temperament or development date supplied.

sources.title: Slovakian Rough Haired Pointer Club — reproduced RKC breed standard
sources.evidence: Authorized primary RKC standard reproduced on club site: versatile field/forest/water worker, tractable/easy-to-train; adult amber eyes and grey coat. Tail explicitly includes an undocked option, moderately high set, down at rest and level while moving. Copyright attribution expressly says RKC reproduced with permission. This supports intact new tail while older FCI320 and selected source show docking.

VBO:0201182.summary: Lively and attentive, the Schiller Hound follows hare and fox while giving voice along the trail. Swedish hunting tradition uses this hound individually rather than in packs or pairs. Its name remembers farmer Per Schiller, whose brother-and-sister hounds appeared at Sweden’s first dog show in 1886; the Swedish Kennel Club recognized the breed in 1907.
VBO:0201182.shortDescription: A lively, attentive Swedish hare-and-fox hound, traditionally following the trail individually rather than in a pack.

sources.title: FCI: Schillerstövare standard 131, English edition 2 October 2017
sources.evidence: FCI behaviour/utilization/history explicitly supports individual work, Per Schiller1886/recognition1907. Prior three cropped/hidden tail references rejected.

VBO:0201182.historicalRoots: Swedish solitary hare and fox hunting; named for Per Schiller and recognized in1907.

VBO:0200441.summary: Dingoes defend their territories and communicate through howls and scent marks, with barking comparatively uncommon. They often hunt alone but join larger packs for bigger prey, sometimes sharing territory during these hunts. Both parents help rear their pups. This ancient dog lineage has lived across mainland Australia for thousands of years, favouring woodland and grassland edges with access to water.
VBO:0200441.shortDescription: Territorial Australian dogs that howl and scent-mark, hunt alone or in packs, and share the work of rearing pups.
VBO:0200441.historicalRoots: Ancient free-living domestic-dog lineage on mainland Australia; woodland, grassland and other habitats.

sources.title: Australian Museum — Dingo
sources.evidence: Actual account sections Feeding and diet: solitary hunter, larger packs for larger game; Behaviours and adaptations: defined defended territory, shared during pack hunts, rare barking/night howling and scent/urine territorial communication; Life history: both-parent pup care; Habitat: mainland woodland/grassland edges with water; Identification: ginger with white feet, erect ears, long tapered muzzle, short body fur and bushy tail. Introduction/Distribution: ancient domestic dog lineage in Australia for millennia. No household suitability, exactindividualpurity, or standard-genetic ancestry inferred.

VBO:0200753.summary: Self-confident and courageous, the Karakachan Dog forms a strong attachment to its household while remaining distrustful of strangers. Its central task is guarding livestock, staying with sheep, goats or cattle rather than gathering them. Bulgarian shepherds preserved the breed through a severe twentieth-century decline, and conservation projects have restored working populations.
VBO:0200753.shortDescription: A self-confident Bulgarian livestock guardian, strongly attached to its household and distrustful of strangers.

sources.title: National Karakachan Dog Organization — Breed standard
sources.evidence: Exact Karakachan standard: self-confident/courageous, strong household attachment and distrust of strangers; livestock guardian working identity. Distinct modern Bulgarian Shepherd identity not substituted.

sources.title: International Karakachan Dog Association — Breed standard
sources.evidence: Original International Karakachan Dog Association standard supports exact morphology and guardian character, whole natural feathered tail and adult proportions.

sources.title: Sider Sedefchev — The Karakachan Dog, field conservation project
sources.evidence: Firsthand2005 Sider Sedefchev conservation account: staying with sheep/goats/cattle, twentieth-century decline, shepherd preservation and restoration/redistribution of working populations; alpine/forest pasture context.

VBO:0200763.summary: Energetic and free-spirited, the Kerry Beagle brings a lively character to scent work. One of Ireland’s two native hounds, it stands alongside the Irish Wolfhound in the country’s canine heritage. Its pack-working tradition includes timed drag hunts; two classes in 2022 had 18 and 26 hounds running together.
VBO:0200763.shortDescription: An energetic, free-spirited Irish scent hound with a pack-working tradition that includes timed drag hunts.

sources.title: Irish Kennel Club — Native Breeds of Ireland
sources.evidence: Irish Kennel Club identifies Kerry Beagle and Irish Wolfhound as Ireland’s two native hounds. No current status inferred from a source crawl date.

sources.title: Continental Kennel Club — Kerry Beagle standard
sources.evidence: Exact Continental Kennel Club Kerry Beagle standard describes energetic free-spirited character and scenthound working identity; adult substantial morphology and complete tail.

sources.title: Kerry Beagle Association — Con O’Leary’s firsthand drag-hunt reports, 2022
sources.evidence: Actual Kerry Beagle Association Con O’Leary November2,2022 group drag-hunt results: two classes had18 and26hounds, timed runs together. Explicitly historical2022 pack-working example, not current2026 schedule.

VBO:0200912.summary: Self-confident and devoted to its household, the Moscow Watchdog combines a pronounced guarding instinct with a balanced, responsive manner. Its working ideal pairs independence with close cooperation with people. Developed at Moscow’s Red Star military breeding kennel in the 1950s, it drew on Caucasian Shepherd, Saint Bernard and Russian piebald hound ancestry.
VBO:0200912.shortDescription: A self-confident, devoted Moscow guardian, bred for a balanced manner and a strong instinct to watch over its household.

sources.title: Russian Cynological Federation — Moscow Watchdog standard
sources.evidence: Actual Russian RKF standard behavior: self-confident, balanced, obedient/contact-oriented, independent, pronounced guarding and household devotion. History:1950s Moscow Red Star program using Caucasian Shepherd, Saint Bernard and Russian piebald hound. Relaxed whole down-curved hock-length tail. FCI-format group is not recognition.

VBO:0200916.summary: Extremely alert, the Mountain Feist hunts with sight, hearing and scent while staying almost silent on a trail. This agile small tree dog was shaped in the rural American South for squirrels, other small game and vermin control. Generations of selection have focused on practical performance, including quick movement over rough terrain.
VBO:0200916.shortDescription: An extremely alert southern American tree dog, tracking quietly with sight, hearing and scent before locating small game.

sources.title: United Kennel Club — Mountain Feist standard
sources.evidence: UKC exact Mountain Feist standard: extremely alert, virtually silent on track, sight/sound/scent, rural South squirrel/smallgame/vermin work and generational performance selection with rough-terrain agility. Revised2020 erect adult ears and complete natural tail carriage; not Treeing Feist.

VBO:0201099.summary: Curious and lively, the Puggle is a companion cross between a Beagle and a Pug. In one UK survey, owners rated Puggles as less attention-seeking and more responsive to training than Pugs; that comparison does not predict every dog. The cross became widely fashionable around 2005, when celebrity photographs brought attention to dogs that breeder Wallace Havens had already been producing for years.
VBO:0201099.shortDescription: A curious, lively Beagle–Pug companion cross, with variable responsiveness to training and a history in the designer-dog boom.
VBO:0201099.historicalRoots: Pug–Beagle companion cross, popularized in the American designer-dog boom of the mid-2000s.

sources.title: Zoetis Petcare — Puggle character and ancestry
sources.evidence: Exact Pug–Beagle companion cross; curious and lively tendencies. No inheritance or universal suitability claim.

sources.title: Animal Welfare — Original UK Pug, Jug and Puggle behaviour study, 2026
sources.evidence: Original2026 Animal Welfare study:48UK Puggles compared with51Pugs; owner-rated lower attention-seeking and higher trainability. Scope is that comparison, not every individual or any health/intelligence conclusion.

sources.title: Fresh Air original interview with reporter Jon Mooallem, 2007-02-05
sources.evidence: Original interview with reporter Jon Mooallem, who had visited Wallace Havens: Puggle means Pug–Beagle cross; Havens had bred them for about twenty years; celebrity photographs around winter 2005 helped spread demand and many other breeders adopted the cross.

VBO:0200316.summary: Cavapoos can be lively and sensitive, with excitability, fearfulness and difficulty with time apart among reported tendencies. Dogs for Autism selects individual dogs of this Cavalier King Charles Spaniel–Poodle cross for assistance training. The charity builds familiarity with everyday settings before teaching tasks such as deep pressure therapy and matching each dog to an autistic partner.
VBO:0200316.shortDescription: A Cavalier–Poodle companion cross, sometimes lively or sensitive, with selected dogs trained for autism assistance.
VBO:0200316.historicalRoots: Named Cavalier King Charles Spaniel–Poodle companion cross with documented individually selected autism-assistance partnerships.

sources.title: Dogs for Autism — frequently asked questions
sources.evidence: The charity directly identifies Cavalier×Poodles/Cavapoos in its assistance training; dogs are individually selected by temperament/intelligence/task needs. Training includes socialisation/settling, public transport/shops and individualized tasks; takes about two years, with ongoing support. This does not guarantee general cross suitability.

sources.title: Dogs for Autism — A dog’s journey
sources.evidence: The charity directly identifies Cavalier×Poodles/Cavapoos in its assistance training; dogs are individually selected by temperament/intelligence/task needs. Training includes socialisation/settling, public transport/shops and individualized tasks; takes about two years, with ongoing support. This does not guarantee general cross suitability.

sources.title: Bryson et al. PLOS ONE original 2026 behavior study
sources.evidence: Original owner-reported UK study985Cavapoos: adjusted scores more undesirable than Poodles for3/12(fear2,trainability); versus Cavaliers differences9/12, worse8 including aggression3,fear3,separation,excitability and bettertrainability. Attachment/attention-seeking,rivalry and touch sensitivity no difference from either. Selected under5 UK population and observational owner reports limit generalisation; no guaranteed inherited parental character.

VBO:0200907.summary: Playful, sociable individuals of this Maltese–Yorkshire Terrier cross have trained for therapy work. In South Africa, Dr Suné Scholtz’s dog Morkie joined children’s play-therapy sessions, responding to hand signals and voice commands. In Indiana, Rocky completed a Love on a Leash evaluation and ten supervised visits, with his handler describing a friendly dog comfortable with adults and children.
VBO:0200907.shortDescription: Selected Maltese–Yorkshire Terrier crosses have trained as therapy dogs for children’s sessions and library visits.
VBO:0200907.historicalRoots: Named Maltese–Yorkshire Terrier cross with documented individually trained child play-therapy and library-visiting dogs.

sources.title: University of Pretoria — therapy dog in Dr Scholtz’s study
sources.evidence: Original university interview explicitly identifies15yearold Maltese–Yorkshire Terrier cross named Morkie. Handler Dr Suné Scholtz describes playful individual responding to hand signals/voice commands and joining child play-therapy work in South Africa. Dog retired2022; no generalized empathy, emotional sensing, therapeutic efficacy, cross temperament or suitability asserted.

sources.title: Suné Scholtz — therapy dog auto-ethnography
sources.evidence: Actual281page original doctoral PDF. Dedication PDFp3 describes her own Morkie playful; PDFp264/printed242 describes child Robyn working with Morkie through hand signals and voice commands, treat-guided hoop task. An auto-ethnography of one therapist/dog/client setting; not a controlled efficacy test or generalized breed temperament. Exact Maltese–Yorkshire identity is supplied by university’s same-author2022 interview, not fabricated as a thesis phrase.

sources.title: Indiana State Library — My journey with therapy dogs
sources.evidence: First-person named handler Paula Newcom explicitly identifies Rocky as a Maltese/Yorkshire Terrier Morkie, adopted April2023. Subsequent puppy/basic classes, CGC and Love on a Leash evaluation, then all10 supervised visits in Grant County libraries, Taylor University and retirement facility; May2025 writer confirms officially in group. Describes this individual friendly and comfortable with adults/children. Prior Gigi is a different pure Yorkie; no Rocky achievement borrowed from Gigi.
